comments.author: @JesusGreenBL
comments.text:
Using a game like environment for these AI agents to interact will also open up countless possibilities for the different ways we interact with them. Imagine if you could watch the agents in real time and see which "room" (i.e. which conversation and with which other agents they were with) they were in, then add or remove agents from those rooms as you see fit, experimenting with different agents with slightly different directives to see which ones produce the best end results. You could even jump into a given room yourself and take the place of an agent for micro-managing aspects of the process. You could add or remove rooms if you felt like the process needed more or less steps for a better end result. You could move agents to a different room to have them brief that group of agents with information about the inner workings of the field they were specialised in. Each room could also have its own database accessible by the agents in it, where they could store information as a form of long term memory. Or they could query databases of other rooms if they were missing some information. You could have a scoring system for agents where they would receive points for completing tasks well or innovatively, and where you could manually assign bonus points when you liked what one was doing. 

The possibilities are endless and I can't think of a time I've been more excited for a piece of technology to take off.

One unsticking strategy I found that GPT uses when coding shell scripts is it falls back to different approaches when you tell it that it failed, for example, I told it to write a shell script to recursively copy folders and contents but leave out files > 1M. I told it that it didn't work, so its solution was to rewrite it as an rsync command, which then worked perfectly the first time. I really think until we get feedback from visual parsing, GUI's are not going to work very well.
